text: Are you being pushed to act right now, or told something bad will happen if you wait?
hint: For example: "your account will be closed today", "pay within 1 hour", "a warrant will be issued".
why: Scammers create time pressure so you don't stop to check. Genuine organizations give you time to verify.

action.text: Ignore any deadline in the message. A real organization will still be there after you check.

text: Did this contact come out of the blue — a call, text, email, message or pop-up you weren't expecting?
hint: Including messages that look like they come from a company you use.
why: Most scams begin with contact you didn't start. That alone isn't proof of a scam, but it means you can't rely on the sender's claims.

action.text: Don't use the phone number, link or reply address in the message. Look up the organization's contact details yourself.

text: Does the person claim to be from a government agency, police, bank, tech company, delivery service or your employer?
hint: Official-looking logos, badge numbers, case numbers and caller ID can all be faked.
flag: Claims to be an authority or well-known organization
why: Impersonating trusted organizations is one of the most common and costly scam tactics. Caller ID, email names and logos are easy to fake.

action.text: Hang up or close the message, then contact the organization through its official website or the number on your card or statement.

text: Is someone claiming to be a family member, friend or boss who is in trouble or needs urgent help?
hint: Voices and videos can now be cloned with AI from short clips found online.
flag: A "loved one" or boss in urgent trouble
why: Family-emergency and fake-boss scams play on your wish to help. AI voice and video cloning makes these much more convincing than before.

action.text: Call the person back on a number you already have for them, or check with another family member or colleague. Agree a family code word for emergencies.

text: Are you being asked to pay with gift cards, cryptocurrency, a wire transfer, cash, or a payment app (such as Zelle, Venmo, Cash App or UPI)?
hint: Or to buy gold, or move money to a "safe" account.
why: These payment methods are hard or impossible to reverse, which is why scammers demand them. No real government agency or business asks to be paid in gift cards.

action.text: Do not send the payment. If you already did, contact your bank or the payment provider immediately and ask them to stop or reverse it.

text: Are you being asked for a password, one-time code (OTP), PIN, or your full card, account or ID number?
hint: Including "just read me the code we sent you".
flag: Request for passwords, codes or sensitive numbers
why: One-time codes and passwords give direct access to your accounts. Banks and legitimate services never ask you to read them out.

action.text: Never share one-time codes, passwords or PINs. If you already did, change the password and call your bank using the number on your card.

text: Have you been told to keep this secret, or not to talk to your bank, family or anyone else?
hint: Or told to lie to your bank about why you're moving money.
why: Secrecy cuts you off from people who could spot the scam. A request to hide something from your bank or family is a serious warning sign.

action.text: Tell someone you trust about the request before doing anything. Secrecy requests are a reason to talk, not to stay quiet.

text: Are you being asked to click a link, scan a QR code, install an app, or let someone access your device remotely?
flag: Asked to click, install or give remote access
why: Links and apps can steal passwords or install malware. Remote access gives a stranger control of your device and accounts.

action.text: Don't click, scan or install. If someone already has remote access, disconnect from the internet, and have the device checked.

text: Are you being asked to skip a normal process — change bank details, move money to protect it, or avoid official channels?
hint: For example: a supplier's "new" bank account, or a caller who says your money isn't safe where it is.
why: Scams often succeed by getting people to step outside the checks that normally protect them. Real organizations don't ask you to move money to keep it safe.

action.text: Follow your usual process. Confirm any change of bank details by calling a known contact, not one given in the request.

text: Does it promise a prize, refund, job, investment return or relationship that seems too good to be true?
hint: Including guaranteed returns, easy money for simple online tasks, or a new online partner who needs money.
flag: An offer that seems too good to be true
why: Promises of easy money or guaranteed returns are a common hook for investment, job and romance scams.

action.text: Research the offer independently. Never pay a fee to receive a prize, job or refund.

text: Does the email address, phone number or website look slightly off, or did they ask you to move to another app (like WhatsApp or Telegram)?
hint: Look for misspellings, extra words or unusual endings in addresses.
flag: Contact details don't match or moved to another app
why: Look-alike addresses and switching to private messaging apps help scammers avoid detection and appear legitimate.

action.text: Compare the contact details with ones you already have on file. Type the organization's web address yourself rather than using a link.

text: Is the message making you feel scared, panicked, ashamed or very excited?
hint: Strong emotions make it harder to think clearly — that's the point.
why: Fear, shame and excitement push people to act before thinking. Noticing the feeling is a cue to slow down.

action.text: Step away for a few minutes. Strong emotion is a signal to slow down, not speed up.
